</table>
</figure>
<div id="S6.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.SS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The routing-only explanation does not survive. Composing the clients’ mechanisms into one program beats keeping
them apart and dispatching (68.5 vs. 64.0%, win 15 / lose 6), and — more
telling — an aggregator <em id="S6.SS4.p2.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">forbidden</em> from writing any domain condition already reaches 66.5%,
above delegation. EvolveNet’s gain is therefore driven mainly by mechanisms lifted into globally shared
behavior, with domain conditioning adding a further 2.0 points on top rather than carrying the
result. The monotone ordering is consistent with both components contributing.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S6.SS5" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">6.5 </span>Does experience accumulate across agents?</h3>

<div id="S6.SS5.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.SS5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The central promise of collaborative harness evolution is that an adaptation discovered by one agent
becomes available to the others through the redistributed shared harness. Aggregate accuracy does not
establish that this transfer occurs, so we measure composition directly. Let each
client’s <em id="S6.SS5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">gain</em> be the held-out items it newly solves relative to the common harness broadcast to it
that round, so that prior rounds’ accumulated capability is not credited to the current clients. On
DS-1000 the five clients’ gains union to 20 items — of which the merged harness retains 18,
a retention rate of 90.0%. Within that union, nine items are solved by the Pandas client alone,
six by Sklearn alone and two by Matplotlib alone, so retention is not an artifact of clients agreeing: the
merged program carries capabilities that exist in exactly one of its parents. Two further items are
solved by the merged harness and by <em id="S6.SS5.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">no</em> individual client, i.e. composition produced behavior that
no single trajectory reached.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.SS5.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.SS5.p2.1" class="ltx_p">A second observation on this benchmark points the same way. Pytorch appears only in validation and
test, so no shard contains it and no specialist exists for it; the unevolved harness and select-best each
solve 8 of its 15 items, while EvolveNet solves 10. Whatever produces that difference was
not learned on Pytorch, which corroborates the mechanism-level reading above: part of what the merged
program carries is behavior lifted out of the domain in which it was discovered.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S6.SS6" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">6.6 </span>How does EvolveNet compare with centralized evolution?</h3>

<div id="S6.SS6.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.SS6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We give the centralized alternative two budgets. At <em id="S6.SS6.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">equal serial depth</em> (<math id="S6.SS6.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T{=}3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T{=}3</annotation></semantics></math> optimizer rounds,
one proposer per round), the per-round-gated centralized optimizer over the pooled 100-item workload
reaches 68.7% on the BIRD held-out; chaining its generations without per-round selection fails
outright (the final candidate scores below the unevolved harness on its own training set and is rolled
back). At <em id="S6.SS6.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">equal total budget</em> — a centralized <em id="S6.SS6.p1.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">population</em> of five parallel proposer branches
per round, matching EvolveNet’s fifteen proposer sessions exactly — it reaches 67.3%: the population
never improved on its first round’s best branch across two further rounds. EvolveNet reaches 70.7% under
the same budget (win 14 / lose 9 against the population baseline on paired items). The margin
on this homogeneous benchmark is within one noise band, but the mechanism difference is visible in the
artifacts: the centralized optimizer’s strongest mechanism helps one database family while measurably
misleading others, so its budget goes into gating a single mechanism, whereas the collaborating clients
develop five specialized mechanism families <em id="S6.SS6.p1.1.4" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">concurrently</em> — and on DS-1000, where that decomposition matters most, the merged harness is 9.0 points above the
strongest single client (Sec. <a href="#S6.SS4" title="6.4 Is this aggregation, or routing in disguise? ‣ 6 Results ‣ EvolveNet: Collaborative Harness Evolution for Agent Self-Improvement" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6.4</span></a>). What this comparison isolates deserves care. EvolveNet differs from the centralized population in two
ways at once: its search is decomposed over shards <em id="S6.SS6.p1.1.5" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">and</em> each branch is instructed to specialize. A
hypothetical centralized optimizer given the same five-way partition, the same specialist instruction and
the same aggregator would perform exactly the computation EvolveNet performs — data locality constrains
<em id="S6.SS6.p1.1.6" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">where</em> that computation runs, not what it is. We therefore read these numbers as evidence that
<em id="S6.SS6.p1.1.7" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">decomposed specialist search plus evidence-gated aggregation</em> beats undecomposed pooled search at
equal budget, and that EvolveNet preserves this benefit without moving any workload off its client — a constraint the centralized method
does not have to satisfy. Distributing the workload is what makes the decomposition necessary and
legitimate; it is not independently the source of the gain.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S6.SS7" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">6.7 </span>Does any of this depend on the model?</h3>

<div id="S6.SS7.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.SS7.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We repeated the full BIRD pipeline — identical shards, specialist instruction, scope-typed merge, gate,
and budget — with the entire model stack (solver, proposer, and merger) swapped from
deepseek-v4-flash to MiMo-V2.5, a reasoning model from a different provider. Every qualitative behavior
replicates: the round-1 merge is accepted with a large gain, a later harmful merge is rejected by the gate
and rolled back, and the final merged harness reaches 72.7% against 72.0% for
select-best and 62.7% for the unevolved harness (EvolveNet vs. unevolved: win 23 / lose 8,
<math id="S6.SS7.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p{=}0.011" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.011</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p{=}0.011</annotation></semantics></math>; vs. select-best: +0.7 points, win 10 / lose 9, the same direction and magnitude as
with the original stack on this homogeneous benchmark). The qualitative behavior of EvolveNet — accepted gains,
gate-rejected regressions, and a final merged harness ahead of both baselines — is therefore not
specific to the original model stack.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S6.SS8" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">6.8 </span>Scaling evolutionary search through parallel trajectories</h3>

<div id="S6.SS8.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.SS8.p1.1" class="ltx_p">An EvolveNet round costs <math id="S6.SS8.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math> parallel local-evolution sessions plus one merger session and one gate
measurement. Client phases dominate wall-clock, and because they are independent the speedup over evolving the same
programs sequentially scales with the number of clients — bounded above by <math id="S6.SS8.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math>, and below it only by
the straggler that ends each round. Serializing the identical client sessions of our runs would take
1.93<math id="S6.SS8.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> (<math id="S6.SS8.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K{=}2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K{=}2</annotation></semantics></math>), 3.96<math id="S6.SS8.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> (<math id="S6.SS8.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K{=}5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K{=}5</annotation></semantics></math>) and 5.37<math id="S6.SS8.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> (<math id="S6.SS8.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K{=}7" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>7</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K{=}7</annotation></semantics></math>) longer than
the parallel phase actually took; the gap from the ideal <math id="S6.SS8.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math> widens as shards shrink and client runtimes
become more uneven — the same shard-size effect that bends the accuracy curve of
Fig. <a href="#S6.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 6.2 Main results ‣ 6 Results ‣ EvolveNet: Collaborative Harness Evolution for Agent Self-Improvement" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>. End to end, including aggregation and gating, an entire <math id="S6.SS8.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T{=}3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T{=}3</annotation></semantics></math> BIRD run takes
6110 s at <math id="S6.SS8.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K{=}5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K{=}5</annotation></semantics></math> against 1693 s for the per-round centralized optimizer and 3655 s
for the equal-budget centralized population. Collaboration therefore does not make a fixed budget cheaper in
absolute wall-clock — it makes a <em id="S6.SS8.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">larger</em> search affordable at bounded serial depth: the <math id="S6.SS8.p1.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K{=}5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K{=}5</annotation></semantics></math>
run explores five specialist trajectories plus an aggregation in roughly three and a half times the
wall-clock of one per-round centralized run, and reaches 70.7% where the centralized alternatives reach 68.7%
and 67.3% (Sec. <a href="#S6.SS6" title="6.6 How does EvolveNet compare with centralized evolution? ‣ 6 Results ‣ EvolveNet: Collaborative Harness Evolution for Agent Self-Improvement" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6.6</span></a>). The aggregation step adds one LLM session per round independent of
<math id="S6.SS8.p1.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math>; gate measurements reuse cached solver calls and add seconds.
What crosses the network is a program of a few hundred lines — kilobytes, a payload whose size is set
by the harness rather than by the model.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.SS8.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.SS8.p2.1" class="ltx_p">These measurements characterize the dimensions along which EvolveNet scales. The search grows with <math id="S6.SS8.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math> while the number of rounds
does not: the client phase is bounded by its slowest branch, so <math id="S6.SS8.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math> concurrent trajectories cost what the
longest one costs (1.9–5.4<math id="S6.SS8.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> below serial). The server’s schedule does not lengthen with <math id="S6.SS8.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math>
either: one merger session and one cached gate measurement per round, whether it aggregates two clients or
seven, although the merger’s input grows with the number of deltas it reads. Each client transmits a harness-scale payload rather than a
model-scale update, so per-client traffic is set by program size, while total server ingress grows
approximately linearly with <math id="S6.SS8.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math>.
And the split is not paid for in accuracy: every multi-client configuration we ran is at or above the
single-client baseline (Fig. <a href="#S6.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 6.2 Main results ‣ 6 Results ‣ EvolveNet: Collaborative Harness Evolution for Agent Self-Improvement" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>). Adding a deployment therefore adds a search trajectory
and a domain of experience to the shared harness without adding a round.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S6.SS9" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">6.9 </span>What the aggregator actually does</h3>

<div id="S6.SS9.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.SS9.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The merge reports make the operator concrete. On BIRD, the server received a value-grounding probe
hard-coded to one client’s database, <em id="S6.SS9.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">generalized</em> it into a dynamic categorical-value probe verified
on three databases, adopted a second client’s SQL-dialect auto-fix verbatim into the first client’s
simpler retry structure, and <em id="S6.SS9.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">rejected</em> four shard-specific prompt rules by citing the specific
graded questions each one broke. On DS-1000, the round-2 merge gated one client’s schema pre-analysis to
Pandas — reproducing, at the server, the same library gating that a centralized optimizer was forced to
discover for itself — while promoting execution-retry logic with cross-library evidence to global scope.
Every adoption decision in these reports cites either a graded per-item verdict or a trace.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S7" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">7 </span>Limitations</h2>

<section id="S7.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Data locality is not privacy.</h4>

<div id="S7.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S7.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Client shards never leave the client — local evolution,
candidate selection, and the per-item verdicts are all computed client-side, and what crosses the boundary
is the harness source, its diff against the broadcast base, and boolean verdicts. That is a locality
guarantee, not a privacy one: a program edit can itself encode client information (our qualitative
analysis shows a probe hard-coded to one client’s schema), and quantifying such leakage requires a threat
model we leave to future work. The method also assumes labeled validation data is available to the server and is
representative of the deployment, a stronger requirement than parameter-space
aggregation typically makes. Finally, the dispatch key that gates <span id="S7.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">home</span> mechanisms must be observable
at inference; it is for databases, libraries and repositories, whereas for the LiveCodeBench check it is
benchmark difficulty metadata — a limitation of that benchmark as a multi-client testbed.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S7.SS0.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Artifact growth.</h4>

<div id="S7.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S7.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Scope-typed adoption adds code monotonically when gates keep passing: over three rounds the
BIRD shared harness grew from 14 lines (the unevolved harness) to 253, and the DS-1000 shared harness from
17 to 409. Nothing in the current gate penalizes a merge that ties on accuracy while adding lines. A strict
tie-rejecting gate is not the answer — replaying it across our runs forgoes 14 items on DS-1000 and
5 on LiveCodeBench (Appendix <a href="#A6" title="Appendix F Gate-Rule Replay ‣ EvolveNet: Collaborative Harness Evolution for Agent Self-Improvement" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">F</span></a>) — but a size- or latency-aware gate,
mechanism retirement, and measurements beyond <math id="S7.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T{=}3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T{=}3</annotation></semantics></math> rounds are needed before claims about long-horizon
accumulation. Our observations cover <math id="S7.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T\leq 3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>≤</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T\leq 3</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S7.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K\leq 7" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>≤</mo><mn>7</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K\leq 7</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S7.SS0.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">The paired comparison is a counterfactual.</h4>

<div id="S7.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S7.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Within a round we score the shared harness that each
aggregation rule <em id="S7.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">would have</em> produced from one run’s client snapshot; we do not run
<math id="S7.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="|\text{variants}|" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mtext>variants</mtext><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">|\text{variants}|</annotation></semantics></math> independent end-to-end runs. This is deliberate — it removes the
<math id="S7.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma{\approx}3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>σ</mi><mo>≈</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma{\approx}3</annotation></semantics></math> client-quality variance that would otherwise dominate — but it means the rows of
Table <a href="#S6.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ 6.4 Is this aggregation, or routing in disguise? ‣ 6 Results ‣ EvolveNet: Collaborative Harness Evolution for Agent Self-Improvement" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> share their client population, and divergence beyond the
round in question is not modeled.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S7.SS0.SSS0.Px4" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">One seed per aggregation rule.</h4>

<div id="S7.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S7.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The aggregation comparison of Table <a href="#S6.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ 6.4 Is this aggregation, or routing in disguise? ‣ 6 Results ‣ EvolveNet: Collaborative Harness Evolution for Agent Self-Improvement" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> rests on a
single snapshot per rule. The ordering it produces is corroborated by the per-library breakdown of
Table <a href="#S6.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 6.2 Main results ‣ 6 Results ‣ EvolveNet: Collaborative Harness Evolution for Agent Self-Improvement" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> and by the mechanism-level retention analysis of Sec. <a href="#S6.SS5" title="6.5 Does experience accumulate across agents? ‣ 6 Results ‣ EvolveNet: Collaborative Harness Evolution for Agent Self-Improvement" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6.5</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S7.SS0.SSS0.Px5" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Label use.</h4>

<div id="S7.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S7.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Labels enter the loop through the local training shards, for client-side
candidate selection, and through a separate validation slice, for server-side acceptance gating. The method is therefore supervised collaborative adaptation, not the
label-free test-time setting of prior harness-evolution work, and its numbers are not comparable to that
line.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S7.SS0.SSS0.Px6" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Ambiguous gold.</h4>

<div id="S7.SS0.SSS0.Px6.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S7.SS0.SSS0.Px6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Within the 40-item hard slice specifically, the audit flags 9 items
whose gold is not uniquely determined by the question and its hint (e.g. the question asks for an average
while the gold enumerates rows). We keep them for comparability with prior work but they cap the reachable
score. All main-text BIRD numbers use this 150-item held-out set.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S8" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">8 </span>Conclusion</h2>

<div id="S8.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S8.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Prior harness evolution studies how one agent improves; this paper studies how improvements discovered
by many agents accumulate in a shared evolving artifact. We introduced EvolveNet, a collaborative
harness-evolution framework in which data-local agent
deployments evolve a broadcast harness along parallel specialist trajectories, and a server composes their
edits into one shared program through scope-typed, evidence-gated aggregation. Once redistributed, that
program lets every deployment inherit the experience the others discovered. Across five evaluation settings the merged harness improves on the unevolved program every client
starts from, and in every setting it also improves on retaining the strongest single client. The per-item acceptance gate keeps the committed
trajectory non-decreasing on the criterion it measures, and on BIRD EvolveNet avoids the stagnation
and rollback that both equal-budget centralized alternatives exhibit. The broader lesson is that the artifact shared during collaborative agent improvement need not be a
parameter vector: an executable program can carry a deployment’s operational experience across
organizational boundaries, provided its adaptations can be composed and behaviorally validated.
Composing such programs is a practical — if fundamentally non-arithmetic — aggregation problem. We
expect the scope-typing principle, and the discipline of grounding every adoption in per-item behavioral
evidence, to transfer to richer agent ecosystems than the ones studied here.</p>
</div>
</section>

<section id="A1" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix A </span>Benchmark Construction and Gold Auditing</h2>

<section id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Per-item gold verification.</h4>

<div id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Every training, validation, and test item passed a benchmark-specific
gold check in our execution environment before use. For DS-1000, each problem’s reference solution was
executed against its own hidden test; 39 of 400 initially sampled problems failed (predominantly
Matplotlib, Tensorflow and Pytorch environment sensitivities) and were replaced by same-library problems
that pass, topping up from the four largest libraries once the Tensorflow/Pytorch clean pools were
exhausted. For SWE-bench Verified, each instance’s gold patch was run through the official evaluation
harness in our Docker environment; all 80 selected instances resolve. For LiveCodeBench, all
110 selected problems carry non-empty test suites.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">BIRD gold audit.</h4>

<div id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">BIRD gold queries are known to contain defects. An LLM auditor reviewed every
held-out item under a deliberately conservative policy whose default is <em id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">accept</em>; an item is rejected
only if (i) the gold SQL fails to execute, (ii) the hint contradicts the question on a concrete value,
number, or named entity, or (iii) the gold silently drops a stated condition or adds an unstated one.
Difficulty is never grounds for rejection: case mismatches between hint and stored data, discretionary
<span id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">DISTINCT</span>, and projection choices are the solver’s job and are explicitly accepted. The audit
is applied during construction of the held-out set, which contains 150 items: 40 hard and
110 representative. Every BIRD number in this paper is computed on it.
We validated the criteria by falsification: an earlier, stricter version rejected 60% of a
human-audited slice, and items it flagged were solved at the same rate as items it passed — i.e., it had
no discriminative power — which forced the weaker, execution-grounded criteria above.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">What the auditor could see, and when it was fixed.</h4>

<div id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We state the audit’s provenance precisely. The auditor’s entire
input is the database schema, the question, the hint, the gold SQL, and the gold query’s execution result.
It never sees any harness, any generated SQL, or any system’s score, so it cannot condition on which
method a decision would favor. The criteria and the resulting item list were frozen on 2026-07-22, before
any of the end-to-end runs reported here were launched (the earliest, BIRD, completed 2026-07-23); the
list was not revisited afterwards. The criteria themselves were developed earlier, and their calibration
used a falsification test on solve rates from earlier exploratory runs, so we do not claim the criteria
were designed in ignorance of all system behavior — only that the per-item decisions were made without
access to system outputs and were fixed before the reported comparisons existed. The audit prompt, the
criteria, and the list of excluded items are released with the code. We have not run an independent human
audit; obtaining blind human adjudication with inter-annotator agreement would be the stronger protocol
and we did not do it.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A2" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix B </span>Shards and Splits</h2>

<div id="A2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">All splits are drawn with a fixed seed (0) and are disjoint by construction. BIRD: five clients hold
24/18/18/18/22 training items covering card_games, california_schools,
formula_1, toxicology, and a mixed shard (debit_card_specializing, superhero, student_club); validation
(100) and test (150) are stratified over eleven databases, four of which have no client
specialist. DS-1000: five clients hold 20 items each from Pandas, Numpy, Matplotlib, Sklearn, and
Scipy; validation and test are stratified over the remaining pool, so Pytorch appears only as a
specialist-free domain; Tensorflow items did not survive the gold check and were replaced from the
larger libraries, leaving six libraries in the final splits. SWE-bench Verified: five clients hold 30 items across django, sphinx,
sympy, astropy, and a pytest+pylint shard, bounded by locally available evaluation images; the test set
adds 10 instances from repositories no client trained on. LiveCodeBench: three clients hold 20
items per difficulty band. ClawEval: five clients hold 8/8/4/4/6 training
items drawn from the workflow, operations, communication, productivity, and miscellaneous task families,
with validation (10) and test (30) allocated from the same families. The <math id="A2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math>-ablation regroups the BIRD shards (<math id="A2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K{=}2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K{=}2</annotation></semantics></math>) or splits the mixed shard
by database (<math id="A2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K{=}7" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>7</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K{=}7</annotation></semantics></math>) with all other settings unchanged.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A3" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix C </span>Prompts</h2>

<section id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Specialist instruction (abridged).</h4>

<div id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Appended to every client proposer prompt:</p>
<blockquote id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.2" class="ltx_quote">
<p id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.2.1" class="ltx_p">“SPECIALIST MODE — you serve ONE client whose data is the slice in these traces (often a single
database). Do NOT aim for a generic harness that works everywhere; aim to become the EXPERT of THIS slice.
Study the traces for the recurring, slice-specific failures […] Encode that specific knowledge —
table/column disambiguation, value formats, join paths particular to THIS schema — as durable mechanisms.
(Still no hardcoding one question’s literal answer; schema- and slice-level knowledge is exactly what you
SHOULD capture.) The server will later merge your expertise with other clients’ — the more your harness
knows that theirs cannot, the more the collaboration gains.”</p>
</blockquote>
<p id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.3" class="ltx_p">The DS-1000, SWE-bench, and LiveCodeBench variants substitute library, repository, and difficulty-band
wording respectively.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Scope-typed adoption rule (abridged).</h4>

<div id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The aggregator receives, in addition to the shared
merge scaffold (deltas against the broadcast base, proposal cards, graded verdicts, line budget):</p>
<blockquote id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.2" class="ltx_quote">
<p id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.2.1" class="ltx_p">“SPLIT EVERY CANDIDATE MECHANISM INTO GLOBAL vs HOME-SCOPED before deciding. GLOBAL: mechanisms whose
evidence spans databases or whose failure mode is universal […] adopt ONE best implementation globally.
HOME-SCOPED: a rule whose evidence comes from ONE client’s home database […] do NOT adopt it globally,
and do NOT reject it for regressing on OTHER databases — adopt it CONDITIONALLY: the harness receives the
domain at solve time, so wrap the rule so it only applies on that client’s home domain. A home-scoped rule
can only change behaviour at home, so off-home regressions are impossible by construction; judge it ONLY on
its home evidence. Still REJECT single-question hacks. CONFLICTS DISSOLVE UNDER SCOPING: when two clients
changed the same behaviour in opposite directions, keep each side scoped to its own home domain instead of
picking a winner.”</p>
</blockquote>
<p id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.3" class="ltx_p">The holistic, quorum, and conflict-resolution variants replace only this adoption block; scaffold,
evidence, and budget are identical across variants.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A4" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix D </span>Measurement Details</h2>

<div id="A4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Two engineering measures make small differences meaningful. All frozen-solver replies are cached on the
full request (prompt, system message, temperature, sample count, and repeat index), so two harnesses that
ask the same question receive the same answer. Every child process runs with a pinned hash seed: without
it, a harness that collects column or table names in a set iterates them in a different order per process,
that order reaches the prompt, the cache key changes, and the sampling noise the cache exists to remove
reappears. Measured directly, the same frozen harness scored 16/17/17 on three identical
evaluations before the seed was pinned; afterwards, two full repeats produced byte-identical SQL on
50/50 items.</p>
</div>
<div id="A4.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Aggregation rules are additionally compared <em id="A4.p2.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">paired</em>. Comparing rules by their end-to-end scores
confounds a rule with the quality of the clients it happened to receive, and the run-to-run spread in the
latter is larger than the effect of interest (Sec. <a href="#S6.SS1" title="6.1 How much does a run vary? ‣ 6 Results ‣ EvolveNet: Collaborative Harness Evolution for Agent Self-Improvement" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6.1</span></a>). We therefore also apply every rule
to the same snapshot of client harnesses and report the shared harness each would have produced, so that a
difference is attributable to the rule alone. ClawEval is graded on a continuous scale by an independent
judge model, so its paired test is a Wilcoxon signed-rank test on per-task score differences rather than
an exact McNemar test on binary outcomes.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A5" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix E </span>Keeping the Strongest Client, Across All Five Settings</h2>

<div id="A5.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Sec. <a href="#S6.SS4" title="6.4 Is this aggregation, or routing in disguise? ‣ 6 Results ‣ EvolveNet: Collaborative Harness Evolution for Agent Self-Improvement" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6.4</span></a> isolates the aggregation operator on DS-1000, where every rule is applied to
one identical client snapshot. The end-to-end comparison against <em id="A5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">select-best</em> — the strongest
client by the server’s validation slice, promoted without any aggregation — was also run in the four
remaining settings, under the same protocol and the same held-out sets as Table <a href="#S6.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 6.2 Main results ‣ 6 Results ‣ EvolveNet: Collaborative Harness Evolution for Agent Self-Improvement" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>:</p>
</div>
<div id="A5.p2" class="ltx_para">

<div id="A5.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A5.p3.1" class="ltx_p">EvolveNet leads the end-to-end select-best protocol in all five settings, and the paired counts favour it in
each. The tests are exact McNemar on the four binary benchmarks and Wilcoxon signed-rank on ClawEval;
combining the five by Fisher’s method gives <math id="A5.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p=0.0027" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.0027</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p=0.0027</annotation></semantics></math>. This comparison contrasts two complete
protocols, so it does not by itself isolate the aggregation operator — the identical-snapshot replay of
Sec. <a href="#S6.SS4" title="6.4 Is this aggregation, or routing in disguise? ‣ 6 Results ‣ EvolveNet: Collaborative Harness Evolution for Agent Self-Improvement" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6.4</span></a> does that. The margin tracks how much the clients’ workloads differ: it is widest
where shards are drawn along library, difficulty and repository boundaries, and narrowest on BIRD, whose
eleven databases share one task shape and whose clients therefore discover overlapping material.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A6" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix F </span>Gate-Rule Replay</h2>

<div id="A6.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Replaying every acceptance decision under a strict-improvement rule (<math id="A6.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="|\textit{fixed}|&gt;|\textit{broke}|" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_italic">fixed</mtext><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mo>&gt;</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_italic">broke</mtext><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">|\textit{fixed}|&gt;|\textit{broke}|</annotation></semantics></math>,
ties rejected) leaves the committed artifact unchanged on BIRD and changes it on DS-1000 and
LiveCodeBench. For the runs whose strict-replay artifact was itself evaluated on held-out data:</p>
</div>

<div id="A6.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A6.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Every decision that differs favours the tie-accepting rule, by 14 and 5 items respectively.
Admitting a merge that neither improves nor damages the validation slice preserves the mechanisms it
carries into the next round, and the artifacts built on top of it are stronger on held-out data. No replay
alters any significance conclusion.</p>
</div>
</section>

  <div class="keyboard-glossary">
    <h2>Instructions for reporting errors</h2>
    <p>We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile
      support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the
      methods listed below:</p>
    <ul>
      <li>Click the "Report Issue" <span class="mobile-only">(<svg role="presentation"
            style="display: inline-block; vertical-align: middle; fill: var(--text-color);" aria-hidden="true"
            height="1em" viewBox="0 0 640 640">
            <path
              d="M224 160C224 107 267 64 320 64C373 64 416 107 416 160L416 163.6C416 179.3 403.3 192 387.6 192L252.5 192C236.8 192 224.1 179.3 224.1 163.6L224.1 160zM569.6 172.8C580.2 186.9 577.3 207 563.2 217.6L465.4 290.9C470.7 299.8 474.7 309.6 477.2 320L576 320C593.7 320 608 334.3 608 352C608 369.7 593.7 384 576 384L480 384L480 416C480 418.6 479.9 421.3 479.8 423.9L563.2 486.4C577.3 497 580.2 517.1 569.6 531.2C559 545.3 538.9 548.2 524.8 537.6L461.7 490.3C438.5 534.5 395.2 566.5 344 574.2L344 344C344 330.7 333.3 320 320 320C306.7 320 296 330.7 296 344L296 574.2C244.8 566.5 201.5 534.5 178.3 490.3L115.2 537.6C101.1 548.2 81 545.3 70.4 531.2C59.8 517.1 62.7 497 76.8 486.4L160.2 423.9C160.1 421.3 160 418.7 160 416L160 384L64 384C46.3 384 32 369.7 32 352C32 334.3 46.3 320 64 320L162.8 320C165.3 309.6 169.3 299.8 174.6 290.9L76.8 217.6C62.7 207 59.8 186.9 70.4 172.8C81 158.7 101.1 155.8 115.2 166.4L224 248C236.3 242.9 249.8 240 264 240L376 240C390.2 240 403.7 242.8 416 248L524.8 166.4C538.9 155.8 559 158.7 569.6 172.8z" />
          </svg>)</span> button, located in the page header.</li>
    </ul>
    <p><strong>Tip:</strong> You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.</p>
    <p>Our team has already identified <a class="ltx_ref" href="https://github.com/arXiv/html_feedback/issues"
        target="_blank">the following issues</a>. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we
      may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability
      should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for
      all.</p>
    <p>Have a free development cycle? Help support accessibility at arXiv! Our collaborators at LaTeXML maintain a <a
        class="ltx_ref" href="https://github.com/brucemiller/LaTeXML/wiki/Porting-LaTeX-packages-for-LaTeXML"
        target="_blank">list of packages that need conversion</a>, and welcome <a class="ltx_ref"
        href="https://github.com/brucemiller/LaTeXML/issues" target="_blank">developer contributions</a>.</p>
